danish.title: Første bog (1805) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Efter at have takket Anna Pavlovna for en dejlig aften begyndte gæsterne at tage af sted.

Pierre var en kejtet mand. Svær, omtrent middelhøjde, bredskuldret, med enorme røde hænder, havde han ingen anelse — som man siger — om, hvordan man træder ind i en salon, og endnu mindre om, hvordan man forlader den med ynde. Han var desuden håbløst fraværende. Da han rejste sig for at gå, tog han generalens trekantede hat i stedet for sin egen og stod og pillede ved dens fjerpryd, indtil generalen bad om at få den tilbage. Al denne klodsethed blev dog opvejet af hans venlige, ligefremme og ægte beskedne udtryk. Anna Pavlovna vendte sig mod ham med en kristelig mildhed, der udtrykte tilgivelse for hans fadæser, nikkede og sagde: »Jeg håber at se Dem igen, men jeg håber også, at De ændrer Deres meninger, kære monsieur Pierre.«

Han svarede ikke og bukkede blot, men endnu en gang lagde alle mærke til det smil — et smil, der intet sagde, undtagen måske: »Meninger er meninger, men kan I ikke se, hvilken ordentlig, godmodig fyr jeg er?« Og alle, inklusive Anna Pavlovna, kunne føle det.

Fyrst Andrej var gået ud i forhallen og stod med skuldrene vendt mod lakajen, der hjalp ham med kappen, og lyttede med kølig ligegyldighed til sin kone, der snakkede med fyrst Hippolyte, som også var kommet ud. Fyrst Hippolyte stod tæt ved den smukke, gravide fyrstinde og stirrede på hende gennem sin monokel.
[På fransk] »Gå indenfor, Annette, ellers forkøler De Dem,« sagde den lille fyrstinde, idet hun tog afsked med Anna Pavlovna. »Det er aftalt,« tilføjede hun med dæmpet stemme.
Anna Pavlovna havde allerede nået at tale med Lise om det parti, hun arrangerede mellem Anatole og den lille fyrstindes svigerinde.
»Jeg regner med Dem, min kære,« sagde Anna Pavlovna, ligeledes sagte. »Skriv til hende og fortæl mig, hvad hendes far synes om det. Farvel!« Og hun gik ind igen.
Fyrst Hippolyte gik hen til den lille fyrstinde og begyndte at hviske hende noget i øret med ansigtet tæt ved hendes.

To lakajer — fyrstindens og hans egen — stod med et sjal og en kappe og ventede på, at samtalen skulle ende. De lyttede til den franske tale, der intet betød for dem, med et udtryk der antydede, at de udmærket forstod, men var for høflige til at vise det. Fyrstinden talte som altid med et smil og lyttede med et latter.
»Jeg er så glad for, at jeg ikke tog til ambassadøren,« sagde fyrst Hippolyte. »Så kedeligt. Det har været en dejlig aften, ikke? Dejlig!«
»De siger, at ballet bliver pragtfuldt,« svarede fyrstinden og trak sin bløde lille læbe op. »Alle de smukkeste kvinder i selskabet vil være der.«

»Ikke alle — for De vil ikke være der. Ikke alle,« sagde fyrst Hippolyte med et fornøjet smil. Og idet han snuppede sjalet fra lakajen — ja endda skubbede manden til side — begyndte han at vikle det om fyrstinden. Hvad enten det skyldtes klodsethed eller var med vilje (ingen kunne afgøre det), beholdt han efter at have ordnet sjalet sin arm om hende i lang tid, som om han omfavnede hende.
Stadig smilende gled hun yndefuldt til side og kastede et blik på sin mand. Fyrst Andrejs øjne var lukkede — han så fuldstændig træt og søvnig ud.
»Klar?« spurgte han sin kone og kiggede forbi hende.

Fyrst Hippolyte kastede hastigt sin kappe over sig — den var efter sidste mode så lang, at den nåede helt til hælene — og løb snublende i den ud på trappen efter fyrstinden, som en lakaj hjalp ind i kareten.
[På fransk] »Fyrstinde, farvel!« råbte han og snublede lige så meget over sine ord som over sine fødder.
Fyrstinden samlede sin kjole op og satte sig i den mørke karet. Hendes mand justerede sin sabel. Fyrst Hippolyte var under påskud af at hjælpe i vejen for alle.
»Gå til side, hr.,« sagde fyrst Andrej på russisk i en kold og ubehagelig tone til fyrst Hippolyte, der blokerede hans vej.
»Jeg venter dig, Pierre,« sagde den samme stemme, men nu blid og kærlig.
Kusken satte i gang, og karetens hjul raslede. Fyrst Hippolyte stod i porten og lo krampagtigt, mens han ventede på vicomten, som han havde lovet at køre hjem.

[På fransk] »Nå, min ven,« sagde vicomten, idet han satte sig ved siden af Hippolyte i kareten, »din lille fyrstinde er meget charmerende, virkelig charmerende — helt fransk.« Og han kyssede sine fingerspidser. Hippolyte brød ud i latter.
»Ved du, at du med alle dine uskyldige miner er en ren slyngel,« fortsatte vicomten. »Jeg har ondt af den stakkels ægtemand — den lille officer, der giver sig kgl. allurer.«
Hippolyte prustede af grin igen. »Og du sagde, at russiske damer ikke kan måle sig med de franske? Man skal bare vide, hvordan man håndterer dem.«

Pierre ankom til huset først og gik ind i fyrst Andrejs arbejdsværelse, som om det var hans eget. Af gammel vane lod han sig straks falde ned i sofaen, greb den første bog, hans hånd fandt på hylden — det viste sig at være Cæsars Kommentarer — og begyndte, støttet på albuen, at læse fra midten.
»Hvad har du gjort ved frøken Scherer? Hun bliver helt dårlig efter det der,« sagde fyrst Andrej, da han kom ind i studiet og gned sine små hvide hænder.
Pierre rullede hele sin krop rundt, så sofaen knagede. Han vendte sit ivrige ansigt mod fyrst Andrej, smilede og vinkede med hånden.
»Den abbé er meget interessant, men han tager fejl. Efter min mening er evig fred mulig, men — hvordan skal jeg sige det — ikke gennem en balance af politisk magt...«
Det var tydeligt, at fyrst Andrej ikke havde nogen interesse i denne slags abstrakte diskussioner.
»Man kan ikke gå rundt og sige alt, hvad man tænker, min ven. Men fortæl — har du endelig besluttet dig for noget? Bliver du garder eller diplomat?« spurgte fyrst Andrej efter en kort tavshed.
Pierre satte sig op i sofaen med benene trukket ind under sig.
»Ærligt talt ved jeg det stadig ikke. Jeg bryder mig ikke om nogen af mulighederne.«
»Men du er nødt til at vælge noget! Din far forventer det.«

Pierre var som tiårig blevet sendt til udlandet med en huslærer — en abbé — og var blevet borte til han var tyve. Da han vendte tilbage til Moskva, afskedigede hans far huslæreren og sagde til den unge mand: »Tag nu til Petersborg, se dig om og vælg en karriere. Jeg går med til hvad som helst. Her er et brev til fyrst Vasilij, og her er penge. Skriv og fortæl mig alt, og jeg vil hjælpe dig, så godt jeg kan.« Pierre havde nu i tre måneder forsøgt at vælge karriere og var ikke kommet frem til noget. Det var dette valg, fyrst Andrej spurgte om. Pierre gned sin pande.
»Men han må være frimurer,« sagde han med henvisning til den abbé, han havde mødt den aften.
»Det er alt sammen vrøvl,« afbrød fyrst Andrej igen. »Lad os tale om noget virkeligt. Har du været ved hestegarden?«

»Nej, det har jeg ikke. Men her er, hvad jeg har tænkt, og som jeg ville fortælle dig: der er krig mod Napoleon. Hvis det var en krig for frihed, ville jeg forstå det, og jeg ville være den første til at melde mig. Men at hjælpe England og Østrig mod den største mand i verden — det er ikke rigtigt.«

Fyrst Andrej trak blot på skuldrene ad Pierres naive ord. Han lagde den mine an, som en mand der finder det formålsløst at svare på den slags vrøvl, selvom det i virkeligheden ville have været svært at give et bedre svar end det, han gav på dette enkle spørgsmål.
»Hvis ingen kæmpede undtagen af personlig overbevisning, ville der ikke være nogen krige,« sagde han.
»Og det ville være vidunderligt,« sagde Pierre.
Fyrst Andrej smilede ironisk.
»Meget muligt ville det være vidunderligt, men det vil aldrig ske.«
»Nå, men hvorfor drager du så i krig?« spurgte Pierre.
»Hvorfor? Jeg ved det ikke. Jeg er nødt til det. Desuden drager jeg af sted...« Han holdt inde. »Jeg drager, fordi det liv, jeg lever her, ikke passer mig!«

english.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: After thanking Anna Pavlovna for her delightful evening, the guests began to leave.

Pierre was an awkward man. Heavyset, about average height, broad-shouldered, with enormous red hands, he had no idea — as people say — how to enter a drawing room and even less how to exit one gracefully. He was also hopelessly absent-minded. When he stood to go, he picked up the general's three-cornered hat instead of his own and stood there tugging at its plume until the general asked for it back. All of this clumsiness was redeemed, however, by his kind, simple, and genuinely modest expression. Anna Pavlovna turned to him with a Christian gentleness that conveyed forgiveness for his blunders, nodded, and said: "I hope to see you again, but I also hope you'll change your opinions, my dear Monsieur Pierre."

He made no reply and only bowed, but once again everyone noticed that smile of his — a smile that said nothing at all, except perhaps: "Opinions are opinions, but can't you see what a decent, good-natured fellow I am?" And everyone, including Anna Pavlovna, could feel this.

Prince Andrew had gone out into the hall and, with his shoulders turned to the footman helping him on with his cloak, listened with cold indifference to his wife chattering with Prince Hippolyte, who had also come out. Prince Hippolyte stood close to the pretty, pregnant princess, staring at her through his monocle.
[Speaking in French] "Go inside, Annette, or you'll catch cold," said the little princess, taking leave of Anna Pavlovna. "It's settled," she added in a low voice.
Anna Pavlovna had already managed to speak with Lise about the match she was arranging between Anatole and the little princess's sister-in-law.
"I'm counting on you, my dear," said Anna Pavlovna, also speaking softly. "Write to her and let me know what her father thinks of it. Goodbye!" And she went back inside.
Prince Hippolyte walked up to the little princess and, leaning his face close to hers, began whispering something.

Two footmen — the princess's and his own — stood holding a shawl and a cloak, waiting for the conversation to end. They listened to the French being spoken, which meant nothing to them, with an expression that suggested they understood perfectly well but were too polite to show it. The princess, as always, spoke with a smile and listened with a laugh.
"I'm so glad I didn't go to the ambassador's," said Prince Hippolyte. "So dull. It's been a delightful evening, hasn't it? Delightful!"
"They say the ball will be wonderful," the princess replied, drawing up her soft little lip. "All the prettiest women in society will be there."

"Not all — because you won't be there. Not all," said Prince Hippolyte with a joyful smile. And snatching the shawl from the footman — even pushing the man aside — he began wrapping it around the princess. Whether from clumsiness or by design (no one could tell which), after adjusting the shawl he kept his arm around her for a long time, as though embracing her.
Still smiling, she moved gracefully away, turning to glance at her husband. Prince Andrew's eyes were closed — he looked utterly weary and sleepy.
"Ready?" he asked his wife, looking past her.

Prince Hippolyte hurriedly threw on his cloak, which in the latest fashion reached all the way to his heels, and stumbling in it, ran out to the porch after the princess, whom a footman was helping into the carriage.
[Speaking in French] "Princess, goodbye!" he cried, stumbling over his words as much as his feet.
The princess, gathering up her skirt, was taking her seat in the dark carriage. Her husband was adjusting his saber. Prince Hippolyte, under the pretense of helping, was getting in everyone's way.
"Step aside, sir," said Prince Andrew in Russian, his tone cold and unpleasant, to Prince Hippolyte who was blocking his path.
"I'm expecting you, Pierre," said the same voice, but now gentle and affectionate.
The driver started and the carriage wheels clattered. Prince Hippolyte stood in the porch laughing convulsively as he waited for the vicomte, whom he had promised to take home.

[Speaking in French] "Well, my friend," said the vicomte, settling himself beside Hippolyte in the carriage, "your little princess is very charming, very charming indeed — quite French." And he kissed his fingertips. Hippolyte burst out laughing.
"You know, for all your innocent airs you're quite the rascal," the vicomte continued. "I pity the poor husband — that little officer who puts on the airs of a king."
Hippolyte spluttered with laughter again. "And you were saying Russian ladies can't compare with the French? You just have to know how to handle them."

Pierre arrived at the house first and went into Prince Andrew's study as if he owned the place. Out of habit he immediately flopped down on the sofa, grabbed the first book his hand found on the shelf — it happened to be Caesar's Commentaries — and, propping himself on his elbow, began reading from the middle.
"What have you done to Mademoiselle Scherer? She's going to be quite ill after that," said Prince Andrew as he came into the study, rubbing his small white hands.
Pierre rolled his whole body over, making the sofa creak. He turned his eager face toward Prince Andrew, smiled, and waved his hand.
"That abbé is very interesting, but he's got it all wrong. In my opinion, perpetual peace is possible, but — how do I put it — not through a balance of political power..."
It was obvious that Prince Andrew had no interest in this kind of abstract discussion.
"You can't go around saying everything you think, my friend. Anyway, have you finally decided on anything? Are you going to be a guardsman or a diplomat?" asked Prince Andrew after a brief silence.
Pierre sat up on the sofa with his legs tucked under him.
"Honestly, I still don't know. I don't like either option."
"But you have to choose something! Your father expects it."

Pierre had been sent abroad at the age of ten with a tutor — an abbé — and had stayed away until he was twenty. When he returned to Moscow, his father dismissed the tutor and told the young man: "Now go to Petersburg, look around, and choose a career. I'll agree to anything. Here's a letter to Prince Vasili, and here's money. Write and tell me everything, and I'll help you however I can." Pierre had been trying to choose a career for three months now and had settled on nothing. It was this choice that Prince Andrew was asking about. Pierre rubbed his forehead.
"But he must be a Freemason," he said, referring to the abbé he had met that evening.
"That's all nonsense," Prince Andrew interrupted again. "Let's talk about something real. Have you been to the Horse Guards?"

"No, I haven't. But here's what I've been thinking, and I wanted to tell you: there's a war on against Napoleon. If it were a war for freedom, I'd understand it and I'd be the first to enlist. But to help England and Austria against the greatest man in the world — that's not right."

Prince Andrew merely shrugged at Pierre's naive words. He put on the look of a man who finds it pointless to reply to such nonsense, though in truth it would have been hard to give any better answer than the one he gave to this simplistic question.
"If nobody fought except from personal conviction, there would be no wars," he said.
"And that would be wonderful," said Pierre.
Prince Andrew smiled with irony.
"Very likely it would be wonderful, but it will never happen."
"Well then, why are you going to war?" asked Pierre.
"Why? I don't know. I have to. Besides, I'm going..." He paused. "I'm going because the life I'm leading here doesn't suit me!"
